slides.visual_description: The Economic & Structural Reality — Identify the major structural shift in physician practice models between 2012 and 2022, and interpret national healthcare expenditure trends and their impact on system dynamics.
slides.narration_text: To ground where we’re operating: two forces define the playing field. The main message is that spending keeps rising to occupy nearly one-fifth of the economy without commensurate outcome gains, which tightens the demand for efficiency and value. In parallel, practice has consolidated—what used to be independent ownership has shifted toward employment in large systems—so influence over resources and workflows now sits higher up. If you want to change care today, you can’t just fine‑tune your own clinic; you need to navigate and shape the enterprise.
slides.duration_rationale: Establishes the two macro forces and why enterprise navigation matters.
slides.narrative_arc: From individual-clinic thinking to enterprise-aware understanding through structural and economic trend evidence
slides.script_notes: The Economic & Structural Reality — Identify the major structural shift in physician practice models between 2012 and 2022, and interpret national healthcare expenditure trends and their impact on system dynamics.

slides.display_title: The Human Cost: System Waste & Burnout
slides.visual_description: The Human Cost: System Waste & Burnout — Recall the approximate share of U.S. healthcare spending attributable to administrative costs and waste, explain the primary driver of physician burnout, and articulate why burnout should be addressed as a system design challenge.
slides.narration_text: Costs climbed and control centralized; that pressure lands at the bedside as waste and friction. The framework here is stark: about 30% of spending is absorbed by administrative waste rather than patient care, and more than 50% of physicians report symptoms of burnout. Follow the flow—waste creates burden, burden drives burnout, and burnout erodes capacity. This isn’t a resilience deficit; it’s a system design failure. The work is to redesign incentives, documentation, prior auths, and workflow architecture so clinical time goes back to patients.
slides.duration_rationale: Walks the feedback loop and lands the system-design stake with two core stats.
slides.narrative_arc: From seeing burnout as personal strain to recognizing it as a system design problem through waste and bureaucracy evidence
slides.script_notes: The Human Cost: System Waste & Burnout — Recall the approximate share of U.S. healthcare spending attributable to administrative costs and waste, explain the primary driver of physician burnout, and articulate why burnout should be addressed as a system design challenge.

slides.visual_description: The Knowledge Explosion & New Technologies — State the current projected doubling time of medical knowledge, describe the gap between AI tool usage and formal training among physicians, and explain how remote monitoring can shift care from reactive to proactive.
slides.narration_text: If waste and burnout are system signals, the pace of knowledge raises the bar even higher—what once took decades to double now turns over in a matter of weeks. The main gap is oversight: about 84% of physicians are using AI‑assisted tools in some capacity, yet only 24% have formal training to supervise them safely. That’s a leadership challenge, not a novelty. The upside is real—remote monitoring is already shifting care from reactive response to proactive intervention—but realizing it depends on clinicians guiding how these tools are adopted and governed.
slides.duration_rationale: Frames acceleration and quantifies the AI oversight gap before pointing to proactive care.
slides.narrative_arc: From technology acceleration anxiety to clinically guided opportunity through evidence about knowledge growth, training gaps, and applied innovation
slides.script_notes: The Knowledge Explosion & New Technologies — State the current projected doubling time of medical knowledge, describe the gap between AI tool usage and formal training among physicians, and explain how remote monitoring can shift care from reactive to proactive.

slides.visual_description: AI Use Outpaces Formal Training — Describe the gap between AI tool usage and formal training among physicians.
slides.narration_text: Here’s the catch: adoption is outpacing education. Clinicians are integrating decision support, documentation automation, imaging analysis, and administrative AI into daily work, but most have no structured grounding in capabilities, limitations, or failure modes. Without that literacy, risk compounds—over‑reliance, missed edge cases, and unrecognized drift outside validated use. Treat AI literacy like a core clinical competency, not an optional elective.
slides.duration_rationale: Surfaces the risk created by the adoption‑training gap and names the remedy.
slides.narrative_arc: From technology acceleration anxiety to clinically guided opportunity through evidence about knowledge growth, training gaps, and applied innovation
slides.script_notes: AI Use Outpaces Formal Training — Describe the gap between AI tool usage and formal training among physicians.

slides.display_title: Examples of Technology Shifting Care and Training
slides.visual_description: Examples of Technology Shifting Care and Training — Explain how remote monitoring can shift care from reactive to proactive and recognize virtual reality as a training modality without patient risk.
slides.narration_text: On the care side, remote monitoring streams real‑time vitals so teams can intervene before a crisis—people with chronic disease stay home longer and avoid avoidable ER visits. On the training side, VR lets learners rehearse complex procedures without patient risk, compressing experience into hours and building muscle memory and confidence. Technology doesn’t replace clinical judgment; it creates the conditions for better judgment to emerge.
slides.duration_rationale: Offers concrete, memorable cases that embody proactive care and risk‑free rehearsal.
slides.narrative_arc: From technology acceleration anxiety to clinically guided opportunity through evidence about knowledge growth, training gaps, and applied innovation
slides.script_notes: Examples of Technology Shifting Care and Training — Explain how remote monitoring can shift care from reactive to proactive and recognize virtual reality as a training modality without patient risk.

slides.display_title: The Consumer Shift & The Digital Front Door
slides.visual_description: The Consumer Shift & The Digital Front Door — Explain how consumer expectations are reshaping access design in healthcare and define the concept of a digital front door in healthcare access.
slides.narration_text: As tools mature, your patients also expect healthcare to feel like the rest of their digital lives—instant access, transparency, and choice. A true digital front door is a unified entry point—online scheduling, symptom triage, telehealth, and the portal—so the journey from awareness to access to engagement is frictionless. Design that journey intentionally, or people will simply walk away.
slides.duration_rationale: Defines the digital front door and frames the journey as a design problem.
slides.narrative_arc: From provider-centered access assumptions to consumer-centered access design through the digital front door concept
slides.script_notes: The Consumer Shift & The Digital Front Door — Explain how consumer expectations are reshaping access design in healthcare and define the concept of a digital front door in healthcare access.

slides.visual_description: The Leadership Gap — Summarize the leadership training gap among physicians seeking leadership roles and identify organizational barriers that limit clinician-led workflow redesign.
slides.narration_text: A great access design still stalls without the right leaders. Many physicians want a voice in decisions, but few receive formal preparation in organizational dynamics, change management, or financial stewardship. Structure matters: siloed governance, administrative gatekeeping, misaligned incentives, the clinical‑operational split, and lack of protected time all constrain frontline redesign. The result is a system that needs physician leadership and simultaneously impedes it—closing that gap is a capability and culture project.
slides.duration_rationale: Names the preparation gap and walks the barrier structure that limits redesign.
slides.narrative_arc: From interest in influence to recognition of the capability gap through training and organizational barrier evidence
slides.script_notes: The Leadership Gap — Summarize the leadership training gap among physicians seeking leadership roles and identify organizational barriers that limit clinician-led workflow redesign.

slides.visual_description: Part 2 Summary & Knowledge Check — Summarize the case for deliberate leadership to translate technology into outcomes and characterize the emerging healthcare system attributes driving the need for change.
slides.narration_text: Pulling it together: knowledge now doubles in weeks, care and training are shifting with remote monitoring and VR, and the digital front door makes access a competitive differentiator. Technology alone changes nothing—outcomes follow deliberate leadership. Your clinical problem‑solving is the asset; translate it into system design. Quick knowledge check: name one way AI, one way remote monitoring, and one way VR could improve a concrete outcome in your setting.
slides.duration_rationale: Synthesizes the case and invites immediate application via a knowledge check.
slides.narrative_arc: From scattered pressures to a unified case for clinician leadership through summary synthesis
slides.script_notes: Part 2 Summary & Knowledge Check — Summarize the case for deliberate leadership to translate technology into outcomes and characterize the emerging healthcare system attributes driving the need for change.
